papers.version_note: QuEra white paper, Version 1.0, June 20, 2023. The text layer lost most Greek letters, many math symbols and unit symbols (the micro sign), printed exponents flat, and fragments some equations and tables across lines. The brief lists no stored assertions.
papers.what_it_is: A QuEra Computing vendor white paper describing the Aquila 256-qubit neutral-atom analog Hamiltonian simulator on Amazon Braket, its datasheet, and five demonstration experiments (single-qubit dynamics, blockaded many-qubit dynamics, ordered phases, quantum scars, maximum independent set).

assertions.value: The authors describe Aquila as a field-programmable qubit array (FPQA) operated as an analog Hamiltonian simulator on a user-configurable architecture, executing programmable coherent quantum dynamics on up to 256 neutral-atom qubits.
quotes: operated as an analog Hamiltonian simulator on a user-configurable architecture
executing programmable coherent quantum dynamics on up to 256 neutral-atom qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor description of its own product, Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that Aquila is QuEra's latest device, available through the Braket cloud service on Amazon Web Services (AWS).
quotes: is QuEra’s latest device available through the Braket cloud service on Amazon Web Services (AWS)
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor statement about its own product availability.

assertions.value: The authors state that all data in the white paper was acquired on Aquila on June 9, 2023, totalling 96,250 measurements over 1,884 tasks.
quotes: All data was acquired on Aquila on June 9, 2023. The data presented in this whitepaper total 96,250 measurements over 1,884 tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the data set it reports, Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that QuEra also provides a private premium access mode with extended machine capabilities and dedicated support.
quotes: We also provide a private “premium access” mode with extended machine capabilities and dedicated support.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor description of its own offering.

assertions.value: The authors state that today's noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) era devices are limited in generality and problem size.
quotes: Unfortunately, today’s noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) era devices are limited in generality and problem size.
assertions.certainty_reason: General statement, no evidence in the paper for it.

assertions.value: The authors state that, even though Aquila has noise and decoherence limitations, there is clear evidence of quantum effects that underlie its operation and its performance.
quotes: Even though Aquila has noise and decoherence limitations, there is clear evidence of quantum effects that underlie its operation and its performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor's description of its own device.

assertions.value: The authors state a belief that noisy quantum computation can be leveraged for near-term applications and algorithms that have a real-world impact.
quotes: we believe that the noisy quantum computation can be leveraged for near-term applications and algorithms that have a real-world impact
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated belief with no evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that analog mode is a key distinguishing feature of Aquila over other contemporary quantum computing systems.
quotes: Analog mode is a key distinguishing feature of Aquila over other contemporary quantum computing systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor self-description.

assertions.value: The authors state that QuEra is building the industry's most scalable quantum computers to tackle useful but classically intractable problems for commercially relevant applications.
quotes: QuEra is building the industry’s most scalable quantum computers to tackle useful but classically intractable problems for commercially relevant applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Marketing statement with no evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that Aquila is a room-temperature quantum device with neutral Rb-87 atoms held and cooled to microkelvin temperatures by laser beams inside a vacuum cell.
quotes: Aquila is a room-temperature quantum device with neutral Rb-87 atoms held and cooled to microkelvin temperatures by laser beams inside a vacuum cell.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own hardware setup, Section 1.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that Aquila's quantum computation leverages four key ingredients: individual Rb-87 atoms as physical qubits, reconfigurable optical tweezer arrays enabling arbitrary arrangements of up to 256 atoms, ultra-stable lasers that drive quantum dynamics in the atoms' electronic orbitals, and Rydberg states that enable the atoms to interact with each other.
quotes: it must leverage four key ingredients: 1) individual Rb-87 atoms as physical qubits, 2) reconfigurable optical tweezer arrays to enable arbitrary arrangements of up to 256 atoms, 3) ultra-stable
lasers that drive quantum dynamics in the atoms’ electronic orbitals, and 4) Rydberg states that enable the atoms to interact with each other.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own architecture, Section 1.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Rb-87 atom hosts two kinds of qubit, a ground-Rydberg qubit that is relatively short-lived but gives strong interactions responsible for entanglement and a hyperfine qubit that gives no interactions but is a long-lived memory qubit, and that Aquila currently operates with the ground-Rydberg qubit only as an analog quantum computer.
quotes: the ground-Rydberg qubit, which is relatively short-lived but enables strong interactions between qubits which are responsible for entanglement, and the hyperfine qubit, which gives no interactions but is a long-lived memory qubit.
While Aquila currently operates with the ground-Rydberg qubit only as an analog quantum computer
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of which qubit Aquila uses, Section 1.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hyperfine qubit states are separated in energy by a transition frequency of about 6.8 GHz and have long coherence (about 1 second), and that the hyperfine qubit will be a key ingredient for a later digital gate-based or dual-mode (analog/digital) operation.
quotes: separated in energy by a transition frequency ≈ 6.8 GHz
long coherence (~ 1 second)
the hyperfine qubit will be a key ingredient for a later digital gate-based or dual-mode (analog/digital) operation
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor description; Aquila does not use this qubit in the reported data.

assertions.value: The authors cite two-qubit entangling gate fidelities of 97.4% for results from 2019 [Levine2019] and over 99.5% for recent results [Evered2023].
quotes: Results from 2019 find 2-qubit entangling gates with 97.4% fidelity [Levine2019], while recent results demonstrate a high fidelity of over 99.5% [Evered2023].
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that Rydberg-basis measurement is done by re-trapping: the ground state is re-trapped while the Rydberg state is anti-trapped and pushed out of the array, and fluorescence imaging reads no atom (0) as Rydberg state and presence of an atom (1) as ground state.
quotes: The ground state is re-trapped by the lasers, while the Rydberg state is anti-trapped by the lasers, quickly pushing the atoms out of the array.
No atom (0) means Rydberg state, while the presence of atom (1) means ground state.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own readout, Section 1.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The text uses 0 for an absent atom (Rydberg) and 1 for a present atom (ground) in the imaging, the reverse of the logical convention used in the Hamiltonian (1 for Rydberg).

assertions.value: The authors state that measurements are destructive, so every experimental cycle rebuilds the atom array from scratch, and that the shot rate is typically below 10 samples per second today.
quotes: every experimental cycle rebuilds the atom array from scratch
While this process is relatively slow (<10 Hz)
Aquila’s shot rate is typically < 10 samples per second today
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own throughput limit, Sections 1.2 and 1.2 cycle description.

assertions.value: The authors state that future systems will integrate methods that do not require complete reloading of the array every measurement cycle, which can feasibly increase the shot rate by orders of magnitude.
quotes: However, future systems will integrate methods that do not require complete reloading of the array every measurement cycle, which can feasibly increase the shot rate by orders of magnitude.
assertions.certainty_reason: Forward-looking vendor statement.

probability. About 600
